schools.summary: Ellicott anchors the accession in 1 Kings 15:24, glosses the name 'Iah judgeth,' and dates the strengthening against the northern kingdom before the marriage alliance of 2 Chronicles 18; Keil surveys the whole reign the verse opens.
Clarke sets the rivalry of the two kingdoms behind the verse: after Baasha's death Israel was weakened by civil strife and Jehoshaphat gained the ascendancy.
Henry: he strengthened himself defensively, not to invade but to check Ahab's growing power without bloodshed, and not by a Syrian league like Asa but by fair methods trusting God.
Gill notes only that Jehoshaphat reigned in the stead of Asa his father.

themes: trust in God not in Syria

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott fix the Hebrew terms — chayil (forces) and netsibim (military posts/prefects) — and tie the garrisoned cities of Ephraim to Asa's earlier conquest at 2 Chronicles 15:8.
Gill: he placed a body of soldiers in the fenced cities to defend them if attacked.
Clarke owns the record's silence: the conquest of the Ephraimite cities is referred to at 2 Chronicles 15:8, but when it was made we do not know.

Ellicott reads 'first ways of David' as his earlier years before Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11), notes the LXX omits 'David,' and takes 'Baalim' to include the calf-worship of Jehovah; Keil agrees the Baals are all false gods.
Henry marks the strong distinction between David's first ways and his last, ruined by the matter of Uriah — Jehoshaphat followed David as far as David followed God (1 Corinthians 11:1).
Gill: the Lord was with him in civil and spiritual things alike; the Targum, 'the Word of the Lord was for his help.'
Clarke repeats the Targum, 'the Word of the Lord was Jehoshaphat's Helper.'

debates.question: Whose 'first ways' does the verse commend?

sides.position: David's earlier and purer years, before the sin of Uriah and Bathsheba
on the LXX text that omits 'David,' the earlier years of Asa, Jehoshaphat's own father

schools.summary: Henry hears in 'sought' the whole of true religion — Jehoshaphat prayed to and enquired of God only, worshipped by God's institution, and would not learn the way of his ally the king of Israel.

Ellicott identifies 'the doings of Israel' with Jeroboam's calf-worship (1 Kings 12:28); Keil reads the clause as a deliberate antithesis — set against the whole pattern of the sister kingdom's worship.
Gill glosses the seeking plainly: he prayed to the God of his fathers, worshipped and served him.

themes: sought the LORD God of his fathers
not after the doings of Israel

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil take the 'presents' (minchah) here not as exacted tribute but as the freewill gifts of loyal subjects at a reign's start (1 Samuel 10:27), and set 'riches and honour' beside David (1 Chronicles 29:28) and Solomon (2 Chronicles 1:12).
Gill: piety is the best prop of government; the throne is established by truth, righteousness, and mercy.
Henry alone gives a reason for the gifts — the people's grateful loyalty for the preachers he sent — and holds that religion is the best friend to outward prosperity.
Wesley: presents such as subjects then brought their kings, in token of respect and subjection.

Keil and Ellicott note that 'his heart was lifted up' (gabhah leb), usually a phrase of pride (2 Chronicles 26:16), is here turned to praise — holy courage in reform; the 'groves' are the Asherim, and 'moreover' looks back to Asa's reforms (2 Chronicles 14:3).
Henry reconciles the removal with the later notice that the high places remained (2 Chronicles 20:33): only the idolatrous shrines were abolished, not those to the true God.
Wesley: his heart rose above discouragement and fear; Asa's earlier removal had been incomplete, or new idols had sprung up in his infirm old age.
Gill: his heart was bent and set on God's ways, fearless and intrepid in the work of reformation.

debates.question: How is the removal of the high places here squared with the notice that they remained (2 Chronicles 20:33)?

sides.position: only the idolatrous high places were removed; those dedicated to the true God were left
Asa's earlier removal was incomplete, or new idols had arisen since
'and he again removed' — a renewal of Asa's lapsed reforms (2 Chronicles 14:3)

themes: holy courage in the ways of the LORD
removal of high places and groves

schools.summary: Clarke calls it a remarkable itinerant ministry of three classes — princes (civil law), Levites (ritual), priests (religion) — making the nation as one man; Wesley shows the princes wielding royal authority to summon the people to God's law.

Keil and Ellicott fix the commission — five lay princes with nine Levites and two priests — and insist Ben-hail ('son of valour') is a proper name like Ben-hesed and Ben-deker (1 Kings 4:8-9), not an adjective.
Gill notes the grammatical possibility that the king 'sent his princes' rather than 'sent to' them, the particle marking the accusative.

themes: the third year of the reign
princes as teachers of the law
the book of the law carried through Judah

schools.summary: Keil names the Levites and priests and frames their circuit; Ellicott takes 'the book of the law' for the Pentateuch and, if drawn from Jehu son of Hanani (2 Chronicles 20:34), a testimony to an ancient law-collection c. 850 B.C.
Gill: with the five princes went nine Levites, and with them two priests.

themes: the mixed commission of laymen, Levites, and priests
the book of the law as the Pentateuch

schools.summary: Clarke: the book of God bound the people's consciences, so they obeyed the laws on the principle of religion; Wesley echoes Henry that the itinerant judges and preachers diffused a blessed light through Judah.
Henry: teaching was the Levites' office (Deuteronomy 33:10); they carried the book both for their own direction and for the people's conviction — ministers should have their Bibles with them.
Gill: they taught the people their duty to God and to man.

outliers.note: Reads Jehoshaphat's itinerant ministry as a precedent for the itinerant preaching of the Methodists in his own century, a means of preserving nations from revolution — an anachronistic application his fellow witnesses do not make.

themes: teaching with the book of the law

schools.summary: Henry makes the verse the hinge of the reign: it was not the army but the fear of God, fallen on the nations when Jehoshaphat reformed his land and set up a preaching ministry, that kept the peace — God's ordinances the true strength of a kingdom.
Ellicott sharpens the word to a 'dread' of Jehovah and reads the peace as the reward of piety (Proverbs 16:7).
Gill spreads the fear over the ten tribes and the surrounding nations, who had learned that the more religious this people, the more formidable.
Wesley: even the heathen observed that the kings of Judah prospered or suffered as they served or forsook God, and so dared not attack.

themes: the fear of the LORD on the nations
peace as the reward of piety

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the participle 'brought' as continual and 'tribute silver' (massa, a load) as hyperbole — 'silver as much as they could carry' (2 Chronicles 20:25) — taking the Arabs for the Bedouin Asa had conquered (2 Chronicles 14:15); Keil simply registers the tribute.
Clarke: the Philistines and Arabians purchased peace by an annual tribute, silver from the one and flocks from the other.
Henry supposes a tribute first imposed by Asa (2 Chronicles 14:14), and fills in a proportionable number of ewes and lambs beside the rams and he-goats.
Gill takes the Philistine tributaries for those of Gerar whom Asa had subdued.

debates.question: Were the payments freewill homage or imposed tribute?

sides.position: an inherited tribute first imposed by Asa's conquests
purchased peace paid as an annual tribute
the continual homage of subject peoples, silver by the load

themes: the fruit of the nations' fear

schools.summary: Ellicott renders a continuous 'waxing great,' notes the rare 'ad lemalah' (2 Chronicles 16:12; 26:8) and the Aramaic biraniyoth (castles, 2 Chronicles 27:4), and sets Jehoshaphat among the builder-kings; Keil takes the 'cities of store' for magazine-towns (2 Chronicles 8:4).
Gill: he waxed great in wealth, power, forces, and fortifications.
Henry: he pulled down his barns and built larger — castles and store-cities for arms and victuals — a man of business aiming at the public good.

themes: greatness measured in building not conquest
stockpiling against the day of need

schools.summary: Keil (with Luther) and Ellicott render melakah 'much store' — property and stocked provisions and war-material (Exodus 22:7, 10) — not 'much work'; and take the 'men of war in Jerusalem' for the commanders only, not the whole host.
Gill reads 'much business' as activity — fortifying the cities and reforming their inhabitants.
Clarke: he kept the people employed at wages, enriching the kingdom; Wesley glosses the business as repairing, fortifying, provisioning, and purging out idolatry and injustice.

debates.question: What does the Hebrew melakah mean here?

sides.position: 'much business' — the labour and public works of an industrious reign
'much store' — the heaped-up goods, provisions, and war-material of the cities

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the muster by clans (1 Chronicles 24:3) and takes Adnah for commander-in-chief; Keil sets out three divisions of Judah and two of Benjamin, with each captain's men 'at his hand,' under him.
Clarke calls Adnah the generalissimo and tallies the five battalions to 1,160,000 in all.
Gill notes the reckoning runs first through Judah, then Benjamin, by fathers' houses.

Ellicott and Keil read 'at his hand' as subordinate — a graded staff under Adnah — and Keil raises the problem that Judah's 780,000 is far too large against David's census (1 Chronicles 21:5; 2 Samuel 24:9), yet the divisions are proportioned.
Gill takes 'next to him' as no mark of rank but mere nearness of place, with the Targum, 'he that encamped next to him.'

debates.question: Does 'next to him' (at his hand) mark subordination or mere juxtaposition?

sides.position: subordination — a graded chain of command under Adnah
mere nearness of place; the captains are co-ordinate, each over his division

schools.summary: Henry: Amasiah offered himself to the LORD, not merely to the king, the most religious of the commanders — offering himself first, and his dedicated things after (1 Chronicles 26:26).

Ellicott glosses Amasiah ('Iah carrieth', vs Amaziah) and the freewill devotion of Judges 5:9, seeing an allusion to a lost act of self-devotion that proves the record's authenticity; Keil agrees the reason has fallen away with the fuller source.
Gill notes only, with the Targum, that Amasiah encamped next to the captain before him.

themes: willingly offered himself to the LORD
the lost source behind the praise

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the armament — men 'drawing bow and shield' — and ties it to Benjamin's ancient character as archers (1 Chronicles 8:40; 12:2); Keil sets Eliada's 200,000 as the first of Benjamin's two detachments.
Gill marks Eliada as the chief commander of the Benjamite contingent.

themes: an army ordered by its arms

schools.summary: Ellicott takes 'ready prepared' (equipped for service) for the heavy-armed hoplites (1 Chronicles 12:23; Numbers 31:5); Keil reads the same Hebrew as the ordinary armed levy with the usual weapons (1 Chronicles 12:24), not specially heavy-armed.
Gill takes the words plainly, noting with the Targum that Jehozabad encamped next to the captain before him.

debates.question: What were Jehozabad's 180,000 'ready prepared for war'?

sides.position: the specially heavy-armed infantry, the hoplites of the host
the ordinary armed levy with the usual weapons, not specially heavy-armed

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes the five generals who 'ministered' at court from the garrison commandants (2 Chronicles 11:11), and reads the vast total not as a mustered army but an estimate of the liable male population — even so, three times too great.

Wesley describes the trained bands whose officers waited on the king; with Henry he grounds the huge total in the Abraham-promise, long peace, immigration from Israel (2 Chronicles 15:9), and God's blessing; Clarke draws the statesman's lesson that religion is the basis of the state.
Henry meets the vast number with covenant, peace, immigration, and blessing — a host credible under the special favour of God.
Gill reads the waiting as done in course, the captains serving by turns, ready at the king's command.

debates.question: How are the enormous totals (1,160,000) to be accounted for?

sides.position: not an army ever mustered but an estimate of the total liable male population, and even so about three times too great
historically credible on the grounds of the Abraham-promise, long peace, immigration from Israel, and God's special blessing

outliers.note: Turns the chapter into a statesman's lesson addressed to the sovereigns of the world — true religion the basis of the state, a religious nation ever great, loved by friends and dreaded by enemies.

themes: the standing forces and the garrisons
the true strength of a kingdom
